first.rationale: We face a compound problem: activation down 6% QoQ and onboarding completion down 4% QoQ. The competitor's pricing pressure is real but secondary to our internal engagement degradation. Memory_31 and memory_86 show that signup simplification and onboarding shortening both improved activation and time-to-value durably. Memory_31 specifically targeted SMB (our threatened segment) with measurable lift. I'm verifying memory_31 and memory_73 to confirm: (1) the magnitude and durability of the signup-simplification effect on SMB activation, and (2) whether promotional pricing in memory_73 showed sustainable unit economics or merely borrowed from future cohorts. Simplifying onboarding addresses the immediate metric decline (4% onboarding completion drop) and directly activates more users (addressing the 6% activation decline). This outweighs promotional pricing because: price-matching a competitor is reactive and erodes margin; improving the core funnel is proactive and compounds. Referral incentives work but require an active base; we need to restore that base first. A standard_experiment scale lets us measure effect size on the current degraded baseline without broad rollout risk.

mid.rationale: Archive verification confirms the decision. Memory_31 (signup simplification) delivered +15% signup, +9% activation, and +4% qualified revenue on SMB with minimal retention risk (-1%). Memory_73 (promotional pricing) shows the opposite pattern: +31% signup and +18% short-term revenue, but -12% 30-day retention and failure to survive renewal—exactly the trap we must avoid when competing on price. Our current state shows 6% activation decline and 4% onboarding completion decline. The simplification playbook directly addresses both metrics with proven, durable effect on the SMB segment that competitors are targeting. This experiment runs one cycle; success here restores our activation baseline and creates optionality for subsequent moves (referral programs, activation messaging, or sales assist). Pricing competition would sacrifice margin and repeat the memory_73 failure pattern. Confidence is high because we have matched prior conditions and the effect size is meaningful (+9% activation directly counteracts current -6% trend).

final2.rationale: Competitive pressure has intensified, but the archive evidence is decisive: memory_73 shows promotional pricing acquired cohorts that failed to survive renewal—exactly the outcome we cannot afford during churn risk. The competitor is betting on price; we must compete on value and activation velocity. Memory_31 proved signup simplification drives +9% activation on SMB. Faster onboarding (memory_86) improves time-to-value and retention durability. Memory_91 shows activation messaging inside the product nudges accounts to meaningful first action. The churn conversations are happening because price-sensitive accounts lack sticky, value-based engagement. A small_guarded_test of simplified onboarding can run in parallel with defensive sales conversations—it addresses root cause (low activation, slow time-to-value) rather than margin destruction. If this test shows activation recovery within 5 days, we escalate. If it does not, we have preserved dry powder for a more aggressive response next week when verification budget resets. Matching price now locks us into a cohort quality problem; improving activation is the sustainable deflection.
